###### By Rick Steves
I spent a week in Shanghai with 100 business and government leaders from Seattle on an educational trip designed to bolster cooperation and trade between our two cities.
With the help of a police escort, our two buses cut quickly through the traffic of this boomtown of 15 million (not counting its "roving population" of 3 million unofficial residents) to the future-esque National Theater. There, sitting under a gaudy sign — crinkled gold foil against a pleated red curtain — proclaiming "Greater Seattle Delegation Welcome" we listened to city big shots while being served a lavish dinner. The menu, printed especially for the occasion, was a grid of Chinese characters 5 rows high and 12 rows wide. Only with the arrival of the sixth course did I learn we were just half way through the meal.
The world's boomtown was in sales-pitch gear as we enjoyed a week-long series of meetings and roundtables exploring ways Seattle and Shanghai might collaborate. Clinking glasses at each meal to spring blossoms and "friendships of a thousand years," this trans-Pacific networking seemed as flowery as it was constructive. Our group of Seattle movers and shakers was struck mostly by how Shanghai was doing the moving and shaking.
Even as they walked us through the "Humble Administrator's Garden" — a classical garden named five centuries ago for an uncharacteristically corruption-free governor — our hosts had an amazing bravado. Their dot-com confidence had some of us musing that "only those who attempt the absurd can accomplish the impossible" — and others pondering a collapse leaving a nightmare of 80-story tall shanty towns.
The mighty Yangtze River empties into the Pacific at Shanghai. How does this city relate economically to the rest of China? "It's as if the Mississippi flowed from west to east, draining America's economy into New York City."
With a trading heritage (from its days as a European colony) unrivaled in China, Shanghai has long been the country's economic engine. In the old days of Communism, Shanghai — considered an evil place — was kept down. Then, in the 1980s, the lid was lifted, and 90 percent of its income was used to subsidize a hungry People's Republic of China. Later, president Deng Xiaoping embarked upon a radical version of Reagan's trickle down economics — the money would trickle from rich to poor — but between regions rather than classes. Shanghai would be given the freedom to grow richer even exacerbating the gap between the Chinese coastal region and the rice paddy interior in hopes that that wealth would seep west. Today rather than 10 percent, Shanghai keeps 40 percent of its profit — enough to keep its engines stoked. With just 1 percent of China's 1.3 billion population, it produces 8 percent of its economy.
Taxis are uniformly polite and fair, taking you anywhere in town for about a dollar. Toilets are called Happy Rooms. Restaurants specializing in duck serve "everything but the quack." Two-story slums sprawl — seeming to clutch bits of traditional life while awaiting the bulldozer.
You need to get things written in Chinese to communicate in this land where the language barrier is as formidable as the skyscrapers. In the market, a tea merchant displayed leaves varying in price from $.50 to $100 per kilo. I asked about the best and she scribbled the local characters for "dragon well tea" into my notepad. Later, stepping past an incense-filled temple into a traditional teahouse, I showed my scrap of paper. For the price of my daily latte back home — a ransom here — I enjoyed the best tea in the house (which tasted pretty unexceptional to me).
Much of China's historic charm and physical heritage was destroyed by Mao Tse Tung's Cultural Revolution — a violent purging of anything not in line with his revolutionary ideals from 1966 to 1976. Much of what Mao missed has been bulldozed in the last decade by the building explosion. The problem is exacerbated by Shanghai's insistence on being modern and western. When I asked about traditional music, both the hotel and the tourist office proposed jazz. When pressed for traditional Chinese music, they explained that would drive local customers away.
The only shows in town were a performance of Cats at the National Theater, the Peace Hotel Jazz band — famous for its ability to play stiff as if Louis Armstrong never existed— and a nerve-wreckingly good acrobatics show.
China has come a long way...but it's far from free. Government leaders are selected rather than elected. Guards and police are posted everywhere. Signs explain the seriousness of "deviant behavior." I could make a cop appear from nowhere simply by sitting on the sidewalk.
Apart from portraits of a dashing young Mao on the paper money and a smattering of newly made Mao pins, little red books, and posters that only look old, there's little physical evidence of the horrific years of the Cultural Revolution. Just as Germans simply didn't talk about Hitler until the 1990s, Chinese conveniently bury their Mao baggage.
This city thrives on deadlines and big events to force progress. Electronic reader boards are already counting down the days until Expo 2010 opens in Shanghai. The government, with a top-down efficiency unencumbered by the niceties of democracy, builds the infrastructure (ports, airports, highways, and so on) in order to let capitalism really sprint. It's the government — rather than the stock market — that incubates new businesses and technologies. While Europeans brag about taking time off, Chinese brag about working long and hard. Members of the Seattle trade delegation (frustrated with the slow pace of change in American cities) were struck — even envious — of how the Chinese talk with clear "move on" words. Americans say, "we'll explore that idea." In today's China, snipers on the sidelines are allowed no bullets.
Historically, merchants were low and scholar/bureaucrats were high in the Confucian social hierarchy. Today, a new generation of business and political leaders — many only in their 30s — is working together (free from traditional class hang-ups and the messiness of democracy) to usher in a bold new age.
To witness all this change as a tourist — even without the royal welcome of a trade delegation — is a thrilling experience. While Shanghai is certainly not representative of China, it is representative of where China wants to go.
Rick traveled to Shanghai with the Greater Seattle Trade Delegation in early April 2003. Did Rick find it an interesting place to visit? Yes. Will Rick be doing more on China? No.

title: 4 Surprising Reasons You Must Visit Shanghai, China
content:
4 Surprising Reasons You Must Visit Shanghai, China - My Family Travels
Shanghai, China’s largest metropolis, exists in a contradiction. One half of this major megalopolis is wealthy and attractive, while the other half is old and rustic. That contradiction may change soon.
Visitors line up to meet favorite costumed Disney characters on parade at the new Shanghai Disneyland. Photo by Attapon Pongpitak for pixabay.
That’s because dynamic Shanghai is addicted to change. Even if you return to the city every two years, there is always something new to see. Just look at the numerous new development projects that take place regularly. For example, your family may not even realize that a very modern Shanghai Disneyland opened in 2016.
Shanghai is part of China’s modern yet traditional aesthetic and therein lies the contradiction. Apart from the fast-paced nature of changes, this metropolis is home to historical attractions such as the City God Temple, Yuyuan Garden and many others. Therefore, you will undoubtedly come across the contrast between the old and the new while exploring the city.
Notice the conflicting manners and contradictory lifestyles that distinguish Shanghai from other modern cities. When you visit Shanghai, you may either choose to live on a budget or spend lavishly. A China Visa is required to experience these contradictions for yourself; click here for more visa information. Read one for four surprising places to learn about Shanghai today.
## The Bund
The riverside part of Shanghai, The Bund, with the Oriental Pearl Radio and TV Tower among the dramatic skyscrapers and ever-changing skyline. Photo by Vineet Pal for pexels.
Your vacation to Shanghai, China should begin in The Bund, where you can join the locals for a promenade or simply observe them practicing Tai Chi. Start your touring early. There are numerous stores, restaurants, pubs and galleries in this area to relax in. The crowds start to build throughout the end of the day. This is for a good reason.
Everyone wants to see the magnificent skyline in Pudong, which is lit up in neon colors. There are thousands of things to do in the neighborhood of the French Concession. Stroll through narrow alleyways and visit various art galleries. You can also eat at one of the area’s many cafes. The French Concession is the perfect place to spend some time as night falls.
## People’s Park of Shanghai, China
People’s Park in Shanghai, China is used by locals for relaxation, play time, sports and — surprise — a marriage market. Photo by Mucahit Inci for pexels.
People can be spotted walking, playing cards, and exercising at People’s Park, which is located in the city’s downtown district. During the weekend afternoons, this park transforms into a marriage market.
Marriage is extremely important in China, and relatives with unmarried offspring in their 20s will be concerned about their children’s future. As a result, the Chinese organize an event that may seem peculiar to outsiders, a marriage market.
At People’s Park, relatives and parents of unmarried adults congregate to participate in an unofficial marriage market. Parents have an important role to play in finding a good mate for their children in Shanghai, China. Be sure to watch as locals gather in the park and use this ceremony to preserve that custom.
## Old City of Shanghai
The Old City or Huangpu section of Shanghai, China with the illuminated stone Customs House. By Dylan Chan for pexels.
The Old City or Huangpu is the area of Shanghai, China where you will encounter the city’s traditional architecture and style. Walk around the skyscrapers and see the older, poorly constructed buildings just behind them.
This part of Shanghai may soon succumb to the glitz and glamour of Shanghai’s addiction to change. Already, Huangpu is falling into the arms of a more modern way of life. Apartment towers, skyscrapers, and shopping malls have replaced some parts of the surrounding communities.
In addition, there is a garden in Old Shanghai called the Yuyuan Garden, which was built as an entertainment center more than 400 years ago. Nearby is the Yuyuan Bazaar full of small shops and teahouses. This area of Shanghai, China is known as the “showpiece” of the country’s growing economy.
## Traditional Temples of Shanghai, China
The Moller Villa, among the old temples of the Old City, highlights the contradiction between old and new in Shanghai.
Photo by Zifeng Xia for pexels.
The Jade Buddha Temple and the Longhua Temple are two notable temples to visit while in the city. Go to the Jade Buddha Temple located in the Anyuan Lu area because it stands out among the city’s temples. The design and gilded statues of this shrine are well-known. It’s hard to take your eyes off the Reclining Buddha statue because this is one of the city’s most revered temples.
Longhua Temple was built during the Song Dynasty and has been well preserved. For obvious reasons, the temple’s architecture is influenced by the Song dynasty. Look for the style that features pointed roofs and unique pagodas.
## Trip Planning Details for Shanghai, China
The Chinese Imperial Palace is among the most traditional of Chinese buildings. Photo by Zhang Kaiyv for pexels.
Visit these temples and other classic sites to gain a better understanding of the contradictions in the Shanghainese way of life. Even while the country strives to develop a modern lifestyle, the people of Shanghai place a high value on tradition.
The Shanghainese make the city a unique blend of modern and traditional. Shanghai has the country’s largest population so it is one spot you’ll be sorry to not include on your China itinerary. Apply for a Chinese Visa now to experience the city’s traditional elements of Chinese culture.
The months of October and November are the best time to travel in the city because it is autumn in Shanghai. The temperatures during this period are comfortable and there are fewer crowds than during the summer holidays and Chinese New Years.

title: Shanghai Disney Celebrates 5!
content:
Shanghai Disney Celebrates 5! - My Family Travels
With the rapid pace of world change, it’s hard to believe that Shanghai Disney Resort is turning five years old this year. We are able to accept that five years has passed quickly. Instead, it’s difficult to imagine there was ever a world without a Disneyland theme park in mainland China.
Mickey Mouse and cast members welcome guests to celebrate the fifth anniversary of Shanghai Disney Resort. Photo c. Disney Parks
Shanghai Disney Resort officially opened its gates on June 16, 2016, bringing the wonder and imagination of Disney to fans and guests in magical new – and distinctly Chinese — ways.
If your family is looking for a safe and exotic international vacation, there’s no better time than this year to catch the Disney magic right in Shanghai.
## Shanghai Disney at 5
In the five years since opening, the resort has become one of the most popular global vacation destinations, with innovative experiences and expansions, including new lands, stories and characters.
To celebrate five years of success, Shanghai Disney Resort has announced a “Year of Magical Surprises” and redecorated the entire resort for fans. This is quite an undertaking because the resort’s Shanghai Disneyland, two themed hotels, Disneytown commercial area and grounds comprise 963 acres. For comparison, that’s about 11 times the size of California’s Disneyland Resort, the company’s flagship which opened in 1955.
## China’s Very Own Disney Resort
Shanghai Disneyland’s Magic Castle celebrates five years with a new light show.
Photo c. Disney Resorts
According to Joe Schott, President and General Manager, Shanghai Disney Resort, the resort has welcomed tens of millions of visitors in the past five years.
The Shanghai Resort experienced a 15-week shutdown (from January to May 2020) to prevent the spread of the novel coronavirus. It was the first Disney theme park in the world to reopen.
When it reopened at 30% capacity, visitors were required to wear masks and undergo temperature checks, as well as social distance at restaurants, rides and other facilities. They still are. Schott has credited the power of positive thinking for making the park a success since its stressful reopening.
## Five Years Brings Many Shows & Surprises
Surprise yourself during the fifth anniversary celebration with souvenirs and gifts that guests can win by using the Disney app as they tour the park. Additionally, look out for special cast members. They will be stationed throughout the park to surprise visitors with a pass to a special “Surprise” show performed just for them in Tomorrowland. Those lucky enough to be given a chance at the “Disney Surprise Wheel” have opportunities to win merchandise, special dining events, annual passes and more.
In contrast with character meet n’ greets and crowd-drawing parades, which have been temporarily suspended at Disney parks due to public health concerns, Shanghai Disney has discovered many new ways to surprise and delight guests while maintaining social distancing guidelines.
## New Events, Music & Costumes at Shanghai Disney
Several new shows with new music and costumes have been created to celebrate Shanghai Disney’s fifth anniversary.
Photo c. Disney Parks
In China, Disney will launch a new nighttime spectacular – ILLUMINATE! A Nighttime Celebration using the cutting-edge technology developed for some of the other parks’ shows.
As Mickey’s Storybook Express gets a new look, a pre-parade of birthday themed floats, including a Disney Surprise Birthday Cake Float towering above 12 feet, have been added. Music and costumes promise to be new for the occasion.
As with all major Disney events, the fifth anniversary of the Shanghai Disney Resort will showcase more than 200 souvenirs with a range of limited-edition collectible items. New menu items and snacks, always popular at Disney parks, will be rolled out throughout the celebration. Expect to see a lot of 5s and sweet treats.
## Shanghai Tourism Welcomes Back Foreigners
In good news, COVID-19 infections have remained very low in the region according to Chinese media reports. Tourism is returning in a big way to Shanghai, one of China’s most popular cities. According to Shanghai’s tourism big data, the city received nearly 17 million tourists during the 2021 May Day holiday, up 138.88% year on year from 2020. Almost four in 10 of those tourists were from other Chinese provinces.
Travelers from many countries outside China borders are now welcomed to visit as long as they have time to tackle several hurdles to entry still in place. Foreign visitors who have completed their Chinese or American-made vaccines may enter the country. Be sure to check with your Visa issuing office for the latest restrictions as additional requirements vary and quarantines are still in effect, even for vaccinated travelers who show negative COVID test results upon arrival.
The continued easing of public health restrictions will increase the numbers able to visit Shanghai Disney Resort as well as the city’s many other attractions.
## Planning Your Shanghai Disney Getaway
More surprises and details about Shanghai Disney Resort’s 5th Birthday Celebrations will be announced in the near future. If you’re going to be in Shanghai, the city has many wonderful hotels. However, none can compare to the theming of the Toy Story Hotel right on the Shanghai Disney property, so it’s worth spending a night there.
Be sure to plan ahead. Go online to Shanghai Disney to reserve your hotel if needed, plus the required entry date and time. This is mandatory for all visitors, including infants and toddlers. Tickets and Annual Passes for entry to Shanghai Disneyland are available via the resort’s multiple official channels.

title: My experience of studying in China, homestay in Shanghai
content:
My experience of studying in China, homestay in Shanghai - My Family Travels
1019086_84090196_270455122I came to Shanghai about three weeks ago to study the Chinese language in a local university. First thing I did when I arrived was to look for a place to live.
As it was my first time coming to Shanghai (and China for that matter), I have no clue what to expect and was obviously lost when I arrived here.
Shanghai is surprisingly pretty big! I tried my luck with real estate agencies (phew, they are everywhere), but it was honestly just a waste of time. They speak little English so I probably spent a good hour making sign languages to them, trying to make them understand what I’m saying. All they did was offer me ridiculously high-priced apartments too (seeing that I’m a young foreigner they probably tried their best to scam me).
Luckily, I met an expat here who recommended me to try homestay. I was skeptical and hesitant at first because I didn’t really want to live with locals but seeing that I have no other options, I thought I should give it a try.
I scouted the web and homestayglobal.com came up. I emailed them and got a response immediately. They arranged a meeting with the host, and took me to see the house. The host family seemed nice and the house, although a bit old, really gave me a feeling of belongingness.
I agreed to stay with the family and I’m really happy that I gave it a chance.
The people I’m with are really nice and regularly cook dinner for me. Aside from improving my Mandarin quicker than what I expected, I was able to learn how to make Jiaozi (dumplings). Mmm.. yummy!
If you’re coming to study, work, or just experience life in China, think about doing homestay; it will probably change your life.

title: Big City, Big Lights: A New Home
content:
Big City, Big Lights: A New Home - My Family Travels
3 Skyscrapers of Shanghai, Representing 3 Kitchen AppliancesThe HuangPu River, Which Cuts through the BundThe Pearl Tower at NightGood morning Shanghai, my second home. The scattered rays of sunlight that manage to penetrate through the thick smog don’t quite do justice to the city, a place better clothed in the sexy black of the night.
However, one of the best ways to spend the day in Shanghai is indoors, in one of our hundreds of shopping malls. Take a walk down West Nanjing Road, and reap the benefits of Shanghai’s international, commerical identity. The world’s finest brand names call Shanghai home, ranging from Tiffany Co. to Forever 21 to Salvatore Ferragamo. You bask in the dazzle of towering mannequins dressed in zipped jackets and tight dresses. The bright white lights of the stores tempt you forward as your brain begins dizzying calculations of cash reductions. When you find the perfect bargain, you leave the store, heart skipping along with your feet.
Though we’re most famously known for our iconic Bund nightlife, also featuring the Pearl Tower (what I see as a kabob lit up by disco lights), Shanghai boasts many artisan hotspots. The best one? Tianzifang. The narrow alleyway apartments that my parents grew up in were transformed into a labyrinth of shops. Right next to the handmade music boxes is a store that sells gramophones and a traditional recipe, fragrant rose hand cream. People move back and forth, shifting against each other to create a rollling sea. As you leave one store to move on to the next, you float along until your eye catches the satirical Mao t-shirts. Don’t leave without buying a few prints from the Hong Lee Shan photography shop. He’s traveled around China collecting shots of Bund sunsets, bustling street traffic, and monks drinking Coke…
After a day satisfying your inner bohemian at Tianzifang, stop by YuYuan garden for the Xiaolongbao (read: possibly the best dumplings the world has to offer.) These steamed delights are pockets of meaty, fragrant broth and your choice of pork, beef, crab, or shrimp.  Take a small nibble and suck the soup out first! Otherwise, for our impatient eaters, beware a burnt tongue.
Here in China’s New York, change is tradition. When I leave Shanghai to return to West Hartford, Connecticut, my hometown, I delight in a respite from the blanketing heat and polluted air. I wait for the mountains of green and blue, dimensionless skies of New England. But when I come back to China for school, I can count on the municipal government to have finished yet another skyscraper.
In New England, I watch as I change and move away from my community. In Shanghai, I seem to be the only thing standing still.

title: 12 Picture-Perfect Spots in Shanghai That Feel Like a Dream
content:

Most Beautiful Destinations Around the World
by 										Jon Miksis
Updated: December 16, 2025

From the peaceful Yu Garden (where I spent hours watching koi fish swim under ancient bridges) to the neon wonderland of the Bund at night, these are the most beautiful places in Shanghai that capture why this city is so incredible. Everyone knows about the skyscrapers, but trust me, Shanghai’s got layers of beauty that most people never see. Let me show you the spots that made my jaw drop in China’s most exciting city.
## Best Places to Visit in Shanghai
Looking for the coolest things to do in Shanghai? Stroll through the scenic Fuxing Park, visit the historic Longhua Temple and Pagoda, and marvel at the breathtaking Oriental Pearl Tower. Explore the bustling People’s Square, a hub of culture and activity. Whether you’re interested in history, architecture, or city life, here are the top attractions to visit in Shanghai.
### 1. Fuxing Park
- 🏆 Best For: Urban explorers 🏙️, culture enthusiasts 🎭, morning exercise fans 🧘
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: French-style gardens, peaceful tree-lined pathways, vibrant local culture with morning tai chi and dance groups
- 📸 Top Experiences: Watching locals practice tai chi at dawn, enjoying seasonal flower displays, exploring the historic revolutionary monuments
- 🏨 Where to Stay: The Langham Shanghai Xintiandi – Luxury hotel within walking distance of the park
Need an Instagram backdrop with cultural cred? Fuxing Park in Shanghai’s former French Concession delivers both style and substance. This unique green space blends European design with authentic Chinese daily life just steps from Xintiandi’s trendy shops.
I’ve never seen a more genuine slice of local life than watching elderly Shanghainese gather at dawn for tai chi and ballroom dancing. The park transforms seasonally—from spring cherry blossoms to autumn’s golden ginkgo trees.
History buffs will appreciate the Marx and Engels sculpture, while social butterflies can join locals playing cards under century-old plane trees. For the quintessential Shanghai morning, grab a coffee from a nearby café and stroll through this urban sanctuary where East truly meets West.
- Morning in Fuxing Park offers authentic Shanghai life with this Shanghai private day tour including Fuxing Park.
Where modernism and Shanghai’s ancient soul meet in Fuxing Park.
### 2. Longhua Temple and Pagoda
- 🏆 Best For: History buffs 🏯, spiritual seekers 🧘‍♀️, architecture admirers 🏛️
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Ancient Buddhist architecture, serene temple grounds, 1,700-year history with the iconic seven-story pagoda
- 📸 Top Experiences: Climbing the historic pagoda, witnessing Buddhist ceremonies, exploring the five main halls with intricate artwork
- 🏨 Where to Stay: InterContinental Shanghai Jing’An – Contemporary luxury with easy metro access to Longhua
Skip the tourist crowds and discover Shanghai’s oldest spiritual sanctuary at Longhua Temple in the city’s southwest. The magnificent Longhua Pagoda, dating back to 977 AD, offers a perfect counterpoint to Shanghai’s glass skyscrapers.
My favorite time to visit is during the annual Longhua Temple Fair when the grounds come alive with traditional performances. For a more serene experience, explore the temple’s gardens featuring ancient camphor trees. Just 30 minutes from downtown via metro line 11, this spiritual retreat offers a necessary pause in your urban adventure.
- Curious about ancient Shanghai? This private tour including Longhua Temple visits the city’s oldest Buddhist site.
Shanghai’s rich history and profound spirituality are embodied in the Longhua Temple and Pagoda.
### 3. Oriental Pearl Tower
- 🏆 Best For: Photography enthusiasts 📷, thrill-seekers 🎢, modernist architecture fans 🏙️
- 📸 Top Experiences: Walking on the glass-floor observation deck, dining in the revolving restaurant, exploring the Shanghai History Museum below
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Shangri-La Pudong – Luxurious accommodations with stunning views of the tower
Want bragging rights for conquering Shanghai’s most iconic landmark? The retro-futuristic Oriental Pearl Tower in the Pudong district isn’t just a skyline staple—it’s your ticket to the ultimate Shanghai experience. Standing 468 meters tall alongside the Huangpu River, it’s impossible to miss.
The tower offers multiple observation levels, including a heart-racing glass-floor deck 259 meters up. Trust me, nothing beats sipping a cocktail in the revolving restaurant as the entire city unfolds beneath you.
Don’t skip the excellent Shanghai History Museum in the tower’s base, featuring detailed recreations of old Shanghai streets. After dark, catch the spectacular light show that transforms this 1990s icon into a dazzling nighttime beacon visible across the city.
Oriental Pearl Tower provides a panoramic perspective of the vast metropolis below.
### 4. People’s Square
- 🏆 Best For: Art lovers 🎨, urban planners 🏙️, people-watchers 👀
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Central urban oasis, harmonious blend of modern architecture and green space, cultural hub of Shanghai
- 📸 Top Experiences: Visiting Shanghai Museum and Urban Planning Exhibition Hall, watching the “marriage market” on weekends, enjoying the musical fountain
- 🏨 Where to Stay: JW Marriott at Tomorrow Square – Towering luxury hotel offering spectacular views of the square
Dive into Shanghai’s cultural heartbeat at People’s Square, the city’s central hub where old meets new in spectacular fashion. Once a colonial-era racetrack, this vast urban plaza now anchors downtown Shanghai between Nanjing Road and Huaihai Road.
The square houses the world-class Shanghai Museum, the fascinating Urban Planning Exhibition Hall with its massive city model, and the ultramodern Shanghai Grand Theatre. I’ve spent hours here just people-watching.
Don’t miss the famous weekend “marriage market,” where parents swap resumes of their unmarried children—a fascinating glimpse into contemporary Chinese culture. With excellent metro connections and surrounded by shopping, People’s Square makes the perfect base for your Shanghai adventures.

### 5. Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park
- 🏆 Best For: Families with children 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦, marine life enthusiasts 🐬, entertainment seekers 🎭
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Immersive polar and ocean-themed environments, cutting-edge marine exhibits, innovative multimedia performances
- 📸 Top Experiences: Watching the killer whale show, exploring the polar expedition zone, experiencing the 4D cinema and light shows
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Kerry Hotel Pudong – Family-friendly luxury hotel with easy access to the Ocean Park
Looking for an unexpected break from temple-hopping and shopping? Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park in Pudong New Area delivers world-class marine entertainment that rivals anything you’d find in North America or Europe. This massive park features five distinct zones inspired by different ocean regions.
The standout attractions include the polar expedition area with its playful penguins and the immersive tunnel aquarium. When Shanghai’s summer heat becomes unbearable, I head straight for the park’s water play zones.
Time your visit to catch the spectacular killer whale performance or the evening multimedia show. Located near Disney Resort and accessible via metro line 16, this ocean-themed park offers a refreshing alternative to Shanghai’s urban intensity.
- Family fun awaits: Book your Shanghai Haichang Ocean Park tickets for marine shows and thrilling rides.
Shanghai Haichang water Park is a marine paradise that unveils the secrets of the ocean.
### 6. Shanghai Museum
- 🏆 Best For: History enthusiasts 🏺, art connoisseurs 🖼️, culture seekers 🧠
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Stunning collection of ancient Chinese artifacts, distinctive bronze vessel-shaped architecture, thoughtfully curated galleries
- 📸 Top Experiences: Admiring the bronze collection spanning 3,000 years, exploring ancient ceramics and calligraphy, participating in cultural workshops
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Radisson Collection Yangtze Shanghai – Elegant hotel near People’s Square with easy museum access
Craving cultural depth beyond shopping and skyline views? Shanghai Museum at People’s Square houses China’s finest collection of ancient art in a building cleverly designed to resemble a bronze ritual vessel. This architectural masterpiece in central Shanghai is the perfect cultural counterweight to the city’s futuristic side.
The museum guides visitors through eleven galleries featuring bronzes, ceramics, calligraphy, jade, and furniture spanning thousands of years. You’ll never see me skip the extraordinary bronze collection with vessels dating to the 16th century BCE.
Grab the excellent free audio guides available in multiple languages. With regular special exhibitions and craft demonstrations, this world-class museum deserves at least half a day of your Shanghai itinerary—and best of all, admission is completely free.

Anyone interested in learning more about China’s diverse cultural heritage can visit the Shanghai Museum.
### 7. Shanghai Ocean Aquarium
- 🏆 Best For: Marine life enthusiasts 🐠, families with children 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦, photography lovers 📸
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: One of Asia’s largest aquariums with the world’s longest underwater tunnel, stunning diverse marine ecosystems
- 📸 Top Experiences: Walking through the 155-meter underwater tunnel, watching shark feeding sessions, exploring the rare Chinese sturgeon exhibit
- 🏨 Where to Stay: The Bund Riverside Hotel – Elegant accommodation with easy access to the aquarium and waterfront views
Dive into an underwater paradise at Shanghai Ocean Aquarium where even seasoned travelers stand mesmerized before the 155-meter tunnel. Located in eastern Pudong, this aquatic wonderland houses over 15,000 creatures from five continents. The dedicated China Zone showcases rare native species you won’t find anywhere else.
I still get goosebumps watching divers interact with sharks during the daily feeding shows. For the perfect visit, arrive early to beat the crowds and catch the morning ray feedings. The aquarium’s thoughtful layout takes you from frigid Antarctic waters to vibrant tropical reefs in just one afternoon.
- Aquarium fans: This Shanghai Ocean Aquarium private tour showcases the world’s longest underwater tunnel.
Visit Shanghai Ocean Aquarium to embark on an aquatic journey.
### 8. Shanghai Zoo
- 🏆 Best For: Wildlife lovers 🦁, families 👨‍👩‍👧, nature photographers 📷
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Expansive natural habitats, extensive collection of rare Asian wildlife, beautiful landscaped gardens
- 📸 Top Experiences: Observing giant pandas, visiting the impressive primate house, exploring the Chinese wildlife exhibits
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Gubei Garden Hotel – Family-friendly accommodation set in lush surroundings near the zoo
Escape the urban jungle for a wild adventure at Shanghai Zoo, where the adorable antics of giant pandas will capture your heart and camera roll. This 74-hectare oasis in western Changning District houses over 6,000 animals in surprisingly spacious enclosures. The star attractions include the rare South China tigers and golden snub-nosed monkeys in the Chinese Wildlife Area.
You haven’t truly experienced Shanghai until you’ve watched orangutans swing overhead in the impressive primate house. Between exhibits, beautiful Chinese gardens offer perfect spots for a breather. My tip? Schedule your visit around the 10:30am feeding sessions when animals are most active.
- See giant pandas up close on this Shanghai Zoo and Zhujiajiao private tour with a knowledgeable guide.
The Shanghai Zoo offers an up-close and personal encounter with the animal kingdom.
### 9. Suzhou Creek
- 🏆 Best For: Urban explorers 🏙️, history buffs 📜, photographers 📸
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Fascinating blend of historic waterfront architecture, modern developments, and glimpses into Shanghai’s industrial past
- 📸 Top Experiences: Cycling along the riverside promenade, exploring converted warehouses, watching sunset reflections on the water
- 🏨 Where to Stay: W Shanghai – The Bund – Luxury hotel with contemporary design offering panoramic views of Suzhou Creek meeting the Huangpu River
Sip craft beer in a converted factory while watching boats drift along Suzhou Creek – this is how today’s Shanghai unwinds. This historic waterway cutting through central Jing’an and Putuo Districts has transformed from industrial artery to urban playground. Weathered brick warehouses now house trendy cafés and art studios.
Don’t miss M50 Art District, where former textile factories showcase contemporary Chinese artists pushing boundaries. Rent bikes to cruise the riverside promenade at sunset when golden light bathes the contrasting architecture. I’ve found the creek most photogenic from the ornate Waibaidu Bridge, where century-old ironwork frames modern skyline views.
- Curious about Shanghai’s riverside past? This Suzhou Creek walking tour reveals historic bridges and hidden stories.
Suzhou Creek is a river with a thousand stories to tell.
### 10. The Bund
- 🏆 Best For: Architecture enthusiasts 🏛️, history lovers 🕰️, night view seekers 🌃
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Iconic waterfront with stunning colonial-era architecture facing futuristic Pudong skyline across the Huangpu River
- 📸 Top Experiences: Dawn photography of historic buildings, evening promenade with illuminated skyline views, Huangpu River cruises
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Waldorf Astoria Shanghai – Luxurious heritage hotel housed in a restored 1911 building on the Bund
Experience a century of Shanghai in one panoramic glance at The Bund, where time travel feels possible every evening at sunset. This waterfront promenade in central Huangpu District showcases 52 historic buildings facing the sci-fi skyline of Pudong across the river. Gothic, Renaissance, and Art Deco facades tell stories of Shanghai’s roaring 1920s.
The real magic happens after dark when both riverfronts ignite with dazzling light shows. For the perfect shot, arrive at dawn when soft light bathes the empty promenade. Nothing beats ending my Shanghai days with a cocktail at a rooftop bar, watching the 632-meter Shanghai Tower glow against the night sky.
- Strolling along The Bund offers stunning views and history on this Shanghai city walking tour.
Shanghai’s famous shoreline, known as the Bund, is its postcard to the outside world.
### 11. Xujiahui Cathedral
- 🏆 Best For: Architecture admirers 🏛️, history enthusiasts 📚, spiritual seekers 🕊️
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Stunning Neo-Romanesque architecture, peaceful sanctuary amidst urban bustle, rich historical significance
- 📸 Top Experiences: Admiring the grand interior nave, exploring the cathedral grounds, attending a service with musical accompaniment
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Hengshan Picardie Hotel – Elegant Art Deco hotel in the former French Concession near the cathedral
Step into a hidden sanctuary where Shanghai’s constant buzz fades into reverent whispers at Xujiahui Cathedral. This magnificent Neo-Romanesque church in southwestern Xuhui District offers a spiritual oasis amid flashy malls. Completed in 1910, the red brick facade with twin spires draws your eye upward.
Inside, soaring ribbed vaults and stained glass windows create a breathtaking atmosphere. The cathedral survived Cultural Revolution damage to emerge as Shanghai’s largest Catholic church. Visit during Sunday morning mass to hear the magnificent pipe organ fill the space. Afterward, explore the surrounding former French Concession area with its plane tree-lined streets and art deco villas.
Shanghai’s varied cultural landscape is exemplified by the Gothic masterpiece known as Xujiahui Cathedral.
### 12. Yu Garden
- 🏆 Best For: Traditional culture lovers 🏮, architecture enthusiasts 🏛️, photographers 📸
- ✨ What Makes It Beautiful: Classical Ming Dynasty garden design, intricate stone and wood carvings, peaceful pavilions and ponds
- 📸 Top Experiences: Crossing the zigzag bridge to Mid-Lake Pavilion, admiring the Dragon Wall, exploring the traditional bazaar surrounding the garden
- 🏨 Where to Stay: Renaissance Shanghai Yu Garden Hotel on the Bund – Upscale international hotel with contemporary décor, panoramic city views, multiple dining options, and prime location between Yu Garden and the Bund
Transport yourself to imperial China without leaving downtown at Yu Garden, where every pavilion, rock, and bridge was designed to surprise and delight. This 16th-century masterpiece in the bustling Old City showcases classical garden design at its finest. The famous Jade Rock – a 5-ton boulder with 72 holes – creates whispered music when rain falls through it.
Arrive before 9am to photograph the ornate Mid-Lake Pavilion without crowds. After exploring, dive into the surrounding Yuyuan Bazaar for Shanghai street food. The famous Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant serves the city’s best xiaolongbao. Visit during January’s Lantern Festival when the entire area transforms with colorful illuminations.
- Worth noting: This full-day Shanghai tour includes Yu Garden and the city’s top historic sights.
In the middle of Shanghai’s crowds, Yu Garden offers a little peace and quiet.
A wonderful mosaic made from elements of culture, modernism, history, and the beauty of nature.

# 13 Budget-Friendly Destinations to Fly from Shanghai in 2025
Jon Miksis
Updated September 15, 2025
Things to Do in Asia
by 										Jon Miksis
Updated: September 15, 2025
466
Living in Shanghai means having all of Asia at your doorstep, and I’ve found some ridiculous flight deals you won’t believe. After months of tracking prices from Pudong and Hongqiao (while stuffing my face with xiaolongbao at Jia Jia Tang Bao), I’ve discovered the best places in Shanghai to catch cheap flights that’ll take you anywhere from pristine beaches to ancient temples.
Want to trade the Bund views for a weekend lounging on Bali’s Nusa Dua beach? Or swap your soup dumplings for fresh sushi in Tokyo’s vibrant Shimokitazawa neighborhood? I just spotted round-trip flights under ¥2000 to both. No joke. These deals are real, and I’m about to show you exactly how to snag them before they disappear.
## #1 tip for finding cheap flights from Shanghai
Looking for cheap places to fly from Shanghai? Here’s a quick tip to save money on airfare.
For the past 5 years, I’ve used Scott’s Cheap Flights (now called Going) to find cheap flight deals. It’s free and super easy to use. All you have to do is enter in your home airport (i.e. PVG or SHA) and where you want to go, and they’ll send you mistake fares and other ridiculously cheap flight deals.
In 2024 alone, I saved thousands of dollars thanks to their email alerts. This includes most recently, a $225 roundtrip fare from Miami to London. On average, I save about $300 roundtrip on selected flight routes. So, I’m a huge fan and couldn’t recommend them more!
GET FREE FLIGHT ALERTS
## Best Destinations with Cheap Flights from Shanghai
Looking to save BIG on airfare? I recommend signing up for Dollar Flight Club. Thanks to DFC, I’ve saved $5,000+ on travel this year…so I couldn’t recommend it more!
### 1. Shanghai to Beijing ($251–$390 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours 10 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Air China, China Southern (multiple daily direct flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: April to May 🌸 and September to October 🍂 for mild weather and fewer crowds
- 🏆 Perfect for: History buffs 🏛️, foodies 🍜, culture seekers 🏮
Beijing is the ultimate Chinese bucket-list city that somehow delivers way more than the touristy highlights you’ve seen online. This ancient-meets-ultramodern capital city packs thousands of years of history alongside cutting-edge architecture and food so legit you’ll question everything you thought you knew about Chinese cuisine.
The Forbidden City isn’t just another tourist trap—it’s literally 180 acres of imperial vibes where you can wander for hours through courtyards that housed emperors for 500+ years. Skip the crowded sections and head to the less-visited northern areas for all the photos without all the selfie sticks. Just outside the city, the Great Wall at Mutianyu or Jinshanling sections offer the perfect balance of accessibility and those epic mountain views you actually came for. After dark, hit up the Wangfujing Night Market for street food that will have you posting food pics that make your friends genuinely jealous.
China Eastern frequently drops fares below $300 roundtrip for midweek flights when booked 1-2 months ahead. May and late September deliver that perfect Beijing weather without the summer heat or winter freeze.
If you’re craving an adventure that’s both unforgettable and budget-friendly, Beijing could be your next destination.
### 2. Shanghai to Hangzhou ($313–$420 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 45 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Shanghai Airlines, Juneyao Airlines (multiple daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to May 🌸 and September to November 🍂 for pleasant weather and natural beauty
- 🏆 Perfect for: Nature lovers 🌿, tea enthusiasts 🍵, photography buffs 📸
Hangzhou is that impossibly gorgeous city that ancient Chinese poets wouldn’t shut up about for a reason. Just a quick flight from Shanghai, this place delivers elite-level natural beauty with its iconic lake, rolling tea fields, and mountain temples that look straight out of a fantasy film set. Marco Polo literally called it “the finest and most splendid city in the world” and honestly, he wasn’t exaggerating.
West Lake is the city’s crown jewel, a UNESCO-listed body of water surrounded by pagodas, gardens, and walking paths that hit different with each season. The Longjing Tea Terraces offer those dream-worthy green rows of tea plants where you can sample the freshest Dragon Well tea straight from the source while locals show you how it’s harvested. For serious wanderlust vibes, Lingyin Temple serves ancient Buddhist architecture nestled against limestone peaks, with giant stone Buddhas carved directly into the mountainside that’ll make your Instagram followers zoom in for a closer look.
Shanghai Airlines offers the best value at around $330 roundtrip when booked 3-4 weeks ahead, although taking the high-speed train can also be optional. Visit during April to catch the peach blossoms or October when the lake reflects autumn colors without the summer crowds and humidity.
Hangzhou whisks you away to a realm where tradition and modernity gracefully intertwine.
### 3. Shanghai to Nanjing ($159–$280 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 1 hour 15 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Air China, Juneyao Airlines (15+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to May 🌸 and September to November 🍂 for comfortable temperatures
- 🏆 Perfect for: History enthusiasts 🏛️, city explorers 🏙️, photography lovers 📸
✈️ My #1 Hack for Cheap 2026 Flights:
👉 Send me cheap 2026 flights
China Eastern regularly drops fares below $170 roundtrip for midweek flights when booked 3-4 weeks ahead. Time your visit in April for stunning cherry blossoms, while October offers perfect temperatures without summer’s brutal humidity.
When planning your next adventure, Nanjing offers both wonder and budget-friendliness.
### 4. Shanghai to Guangzhou ($179–$300 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours 40 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Southern, Spring Airlines, China Eastern (20+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: October to December 🍂 and March to May 🌸 for mild temperatures
- 🏆 Perfect for: Food lovers 🍲, urban explorers 🏙️, shopping enthusiasts 🛍️
Guangzhou is China’s ultimate food paradise that serious travelers know not to skip. This southern metropolis brings next-level Cantonese cuisine, ultramodern architecture, and tropical vibes that feel worlds away from Shanghai. It’s basically the gateway to understanding why Cantonese food conquered the globe while still keeping its best secrets for locals.
The Canton Tower isn’t just another city observation deck. This 600-meter twisting structure lights up with wild LED displays at night and has a glass-bottom walkway that will literally test your fear of heights. For food adventures, skip the tourist spots and head straight to Shangxiajiu Pedestrian Street where you can sample everything from dim sum to wok-fried specialties that redefine what you thought Chinese food could be. When the urban intensity gets too much, Baiyun Mountain offers lush hiking trails and sweeping city views, while the Chen Clan Ancestral Hall brings traditional architecture and incredible folk art without the usual tourist crowds.
November and March give you perfect subtropical weather without summer’s intense heat and humidity. For flights from Shanghai, Spring Airlines offers the best value with fares starting around $179 roundtrip when booked 4-6 weeks ahead.
For a Guangzhou getaway, aim for spring or autumn—the optimal seasons.
### 5. Shanghai to Shenzhen ($213–$340 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours 45 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Southern, Shenzhen Airlines, Spring Airlines (15+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: October to December 🍁 and March to April 🌼 for comfortable weather
- 🏆 Perfect for: Tech enthusiasts 💻, design lovers 🎨, border hoppers 🌉
Shenzhen is literally the fastest-growing city you’ve never properly considered. This former fishing village transformed into China’s Silicon Valley in just four decades, creating a playground of futuristic architecture, cutting-edge tech, and a design scene that’s reshaping global trends. It’s where tomorrow’s gadgets get made today.
OCT Loft delivers serious creative district energy with converted industrial spaces now filled with design studios, art galleries, and coffee shops where China’s digital nomads tap away on laptops. For mind-blowing shopping, Huaqiangbei Electronics Market spans multiple buildings packed with every tech component imaginable, from smartphone parts to DIY drone kits at prices that’ll make you question everything you’ve ever paid for electronics. When you need nature vibes, Lianhuashan Park offers hilltop views of the impressive skyline, while Window of the World brings hilariously scaled-down versions of global landmarks that are somehow both tacky and totally worth visiting.
Shenzhen Airlines frequently offers fares around $240 roundtrip when booked 2-3 months ahead, with best deals on Tuesday and Wednesday departures. November hits the sweet spot with perfect temperatures and clear skies for cityscape photos.
When in search of an affordable yet awe-inspiring destination, let Shenzhen inspire your journey.
### 6. Shanghai to Chengdu ($266–$390 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 3 hours 15 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: Sichuan Airlines, China Eastern, Air China (12+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to May 🌸 and September to November 🍂 for mild weather
- 🏆 Perfect for: Panda lovers 🐼, food adventurers 🌶️, culture seekers 🏮
Chengdu is that rare city where ancient traditions and modern chill vibes perfectly coexist. This Sichuan capital delivers the iconic panda experience you secretly came to China for, plus food so intensely flavorful it will literally numb your face and a teahouse culture that elevates relaxation to an art form.
Sichuan Airlines offers direct flights starting around $280 roundtrip when booked 6-8 weeks ahead. April brings perfect weather for panda viewing without summer crowds, while October offers clear skies and comfortable temperatures. Avoid Chinese New Year unless you enjoy paying triple for everything.
When the wanderlust strikes, and you desire an exceptional and cost-effective getaway, consider Chengdu as your next destination.
### 7. Shanghai to Xi’an ($240–$360 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours 30 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Hainan Airlines, Spring Airlines (10+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to May 🌸 and September to November 🍂 for pleasant weather
- 🏆 Perfect for: History obsessives 🏛️, food adventurers 🍜, ancient culture fans 🏮
The Terracotta Warriors aren’t just some tourist trap. This literal army of 8,000+ unique clay soldiers was buried for over 2,000 years before farmers accidentally discovered them in 1974. For food that will blow your mind, the Muslim Quarter serves up hand-pulled noodles, cumin-spiced lamb skewers, and persimmon cakes in a street food paradise where recipes haven’t changed in centuries. When you’re ready to walk off all that food, the Ancient City Wall offers bike rentals for cruising above the city with views that perfectly contrast old and new Xi’an.
Hainan Airlines regularly drops fares below $260 roundtrip for midweek flights when booked 2-3 months ahead. Visit around April for stunning spring weather without summer crowds, or October for perfect outdoor temperatures.
Welcome to Xi’an, where history springs to life!
### 8. Shanghai to Qingdao ($155–$260 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 1 hour 35 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Juneyao Airlines, Qingdao Airlines (8+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: May to October 🌞 for beach weather and seafood season
- 🏆 Perfect for: Beach lovers 🏖️, beer enthusiasts 🍺, seafood fanatics 🦞
Qingdao is China’s unexpected coastal gem that somehow combines German colonial architecture, pristine beaches, and beer culture into one seriously underrated package. This seaside city brings harbor views that could pass for Europe, seafood so fresh it was swimming hours ago, and a laid-back vibe that feels miles away from China’s megacities.
Qingdao Airlines offers seasonal deals as low as $155 roundtrip during shoulder months when booked 4-6 weeks out. Summer brings perfect beach weather but expect weekend crowds escaping Shanghai’s heat. Early October serves up the famous Qingdao International Beer Festival (think Chinese Oktoberfest) with beer tents, live music, and endless food stalls.
When wanderlust beckons and you crave a distinctive yet budget-friendly escape, consider Qingdao as your destination.
### 9. Shanghai to Wuhan ($214–$330 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 1 hour 50 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, China Southern, Juneyao Airlines (10+ daily flights)
- 🏆 Perfect for: History buffs 🏛️, college town explorers 🎓, river culture fans 🚢
Wuhan is that off-the-beaten-path city where three towns merged into one epic metropolis straddling the mighty Yangtze River. This university hub gives serious cultural depth without the tourist crowds, with stunning lakes, revolutionary history, and a spicy food scene that rivals Chengdu but somehow still flies under the radar.
East Lake serves premium natural vibes with its massive scenic area spanning 33 square kilometers, where you’ll find cherry blossoms in spring that give Japan a run for its money. For history that hits different, the Yellow Crane Tower delivers those classic Chinese pagoda views you’ve been craving, perched on Snake Hill with panoramas across the entire city. When night falls, Hubu Alley transforms into a buzzing street food paradise where locals feast on “hot dry noodles” (the city’s signature breakfast dish that’s actually perfect anytime) and spicy duck necks that might become your new obsession.
Juneyao Airlines typically offers the best deals around $220 roundtrip when booked 2-3 months in advance.
Wuhan’s real allure lies in its skillful fusion of the ancient and the contemporary.
### 10. Shanghai to Chongqing ($199–$310 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours 50 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: Sichuan Airlines, China Eastern, Spring Airlines (8+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to April 🌸 and October to November 🍂 for clear skies
- 🏆 Perfect for: Urban explorers 🏙️, spicy food lovers 🌶️, river cruise enthusiasts 🚢
Hongyadong gives major cyberpunk vibes with its 11-story stilt house complex built into the mountainside, lit up at night in ways that break your camera’s HDR settings. For those insane city views you’ve seen on social media, Liziba Station is where subway trains actually pass through the middle of a residential building, while Raffles City offers glass-bottomed sky bridges connecting six skyscrapers 250 meters above ground.
Spring Airlines regularly drops fares to around $220 roundtrip when you target midweek departures and book 1-2 months ahead. Plan your visit for November when the notorious Chongqing fog lifts enough to actually see the dramatic cityscape without summer’s sweltering humidity.
As one of the cheap countries to fly from Shanghai, Chongqing assures both excitement and affordability.
### 11. Shanghai to Kunming ($210–$320 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 3 hours 20 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Eastern, Lucky Air, Spring Airlines (7+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: March to June 🌼 and September to November 🍂 for ideal exploring weather
- 🏆 Perfect for: Nature enthusiasts 🏞️, ethnic culture seekers 🏮, photography lovers 📸
Kunming is China’s best-kept secret that should be way more famous than it is. This chilled-out city sits at the perfect elevation where it’s never too hot or too cold, surrounded by insane landscapes that look photoshopped and cultural diversity that makes the rest of China seem boring. It’s usually where Chinese people vacation when they’re tired of crowds and want perfect weather.
Lucky Air typically offers the most wallet-friendly fares hovering around $230 roundtrip when you lock in prices 6-8 weeks before departure. Consider exploring in late March when pink cherry blossoms blanket the city or target mid-October when crystal clear skies create perfect conditions for those Stone Forest photos.
Known as the “City of Eternal Spring,” Kunming enchants with its mild climate and stunning scenery.
### 12. Shanghai to Taipei ($289–$420 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 1 hour 45 minutes
- 🛫 Airlines: China Airlines, EVA Air, Spring Airlines (multiple daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: October to April 🍂 for pleasant temperatures and fewer rain showers
- 🏆 Perfect for: Food adventurers 🍜, night market enthusiasts 🏮, culture seekers 🏛️
Taipei is that perfect-sized city that hits different from anywhere else in the Chinese-speaking world. This food-obsessed capital delivers night markets that will ruin street food for you forever, a skyline anchored by that iconic bamboo-shaped skyscraper, and cultural vibes that blend Chinese traditions with Japanese influences and its own unique identity.
EVA Air offers the most reliable service with fares starting around $310 roundtrip, though budget hunters should watch for Spring Airlines deals that occasionally drop below $300 when booked 2-3 months ahead. Score the best weather between November and February when Taipei chills out with comfortable temperatures and significantly less rainfall than its notoriously wet summers.
As one of the cheap countries to fly from Shanghai, Taipei combines tradition and modernity seamlessly
### 13. Shanghai to Seoul ($211–$350 roundtrip)
- ✈️ Flight Time: 2 hours
- 🛫 Airlines: Korean Air, China Eastern, Asiana Airlines (10+ daily flights)
- 📅 Best Time to Visit: April to June 🌸 and September to November 🍁 for mild weather
- 🏆 Perfect for: K-culture fanatics 🎭, shopping addicts 🛍️, food scene explorers 🍜
Seoul is that electric fusion city where centuries-old tradition crashes into cutting-edge tech on every street corner. This K-wave epicenter delivers a fashion scene so forward-thinking your Instagram will feel dated before you even post, a food culture that ranges from royal court cuisines to late-night pojangmacha tents, and a beauty industry that’s literally years ahead of everyone else.
Changdeokgung Palace isn’t just another historic site but a UNESCO gem with its secret garden that changes dramatically with each season. When hunger strikes, Gwangjang Market serves up authentic street food where you can watch grandmas who’ve been making the same perfect bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes) for decades. For K-culture immersion, Hongdae buzzes with underground music venues, quirky cafés, and street performers creating that perfect Seoul energy that makes time disappear until you suddenly realize it’s 3am.
T’way Air and Juneyao Airlines battle for the budget crown with occasional fare drops below $220 roundtrip during shoulder season. Hit town during cherry blossom madness in early April when the city transforms into a pink wonderland, or target early November when fall foliage creates golden backdrops for your palace photos.
Seoul is a city pulsing with vitality, where traditional tea houses harmonize with cutting-edge design studios.
You can definitely find the cheapest places to fly from Shanghai with ease!

Jon Miksis
Updated February 9, 2025
Most Beautiful Destinations Around the World
by 										Jon Miksis
Updated: February 9, 2025
13.2K
This isn’t your standard “must-see” list of tourist spots. Sure, I’ll tell you where to find the best view of the Pudong skyline, but also why you should skip the tourist-packed Yu Garden at noon and come back at 8 AM instead. From getting wonderfully lost in the French Concession’s plane tree-lined streets to knowing exactly which xiaolongbao spot will change your life forever, here are my seven tried-and-tested experiences that’ll help you crack the code to this magnificent chaos of a city.
## 📌 Visiting Shanghai at a Glance
Shanghai is a city of a superlatives. With over 24 million people, Shanghai is the largest city in China and the second largest city proper in the world. It has the world’s fastest passenger train, the Shanghai Maglev, zipping at 267 miles/hour (430 kilometers/hour). Shanghai also has the second tallest building in the world, the Shanghai Tower, which stands 2,073 feet (632 meters) tall.
Here are some highlights:
### 🌟 Top 7 Must-See Attractions in Shanghai:
🔹 The Bund – Iconic waterfront with stunning skyline views.🔹 Yu Garden – A classical Chinese garden with intricate pavilions.🔹 Tianzifang & Xintiandi – Trendy shopping & dining spots in the French Concession.🔹 Shanghai Museum – China’s finest collection of ancient art and artifacts.🔹 Oriental Pearl Tower – A futuristic tower with glass-bottomed observation decks.🔹 Jing’an Temple – A stunning Buddhist temple amidst skyscrapers.🔹 Nanjing Road – One of the world’s busiest shopping streets.
### 🗓️ Essential Shanghai Travel Info
✔ Best Time to Visit Shanghai – A breakdown of seasons, weather, and events to help you plan your trip.✔ Shanghai Travel Pass & Budgeting Tips – A guide to saving money on transport, attractions, and food.✔ Day Trips from Shanghai – The best short trips within 1-2 hours, including Hangzhou, Suzhou, and ancient water towns.✔ China Travel Tips & Advice – Essential visa info, cultural tips, and key Mandarin phrases.
As a commercial and cultural center, Shanghai offers a variety of impressive tourist sites. Based on my recent trip to Shanghai, here are the top 7 attractions and things to do that you can’t miss!

Here’s a map with the top attractions in Shanghai.

## Best Time to Visit Shanghai in 2025
Shanghai is a year-round destination, but each season offers a different experience. Here’s a detailed breakdown of weather, crowds, and key events to help you choose the best time to visit.
### 🌸 Spring (March – May) – Best Overall Weather & Cherry Blossoms
✅ Why Visit? Spring in Shanghai is mild, pleasant, and colorful, with blooming cherry blossoms and comfortable sightseeing weather.
🌡️ Temperature: 50-75°F (10-24°C)🚶 Crowds: Moderate (busier in April due to local holidays)🎭 Key Events:
- Shanghai International Film Festival (March) – Asia’s version of Cannes.
- Peach Blossom Festival (March-April) – Best viewed in Nanhui Peach Blossom Village.
- Qingming Festival (Early April) – “Tomb Sweeping Day” when locals honor ancestors.
🛑 Avoid: The first week of April (Qingming Festival) when locals travel.
### ☀️ Summer (June – August) – Hot, Humid & Typhoon Season
✅ Why Visit? This is peak travel season with extended daylight hours, lively nightlife, and major festivals. However, heat and humidity are intense, and prices are higher.
🌡️ Temperature: 80-100°F (27-38°C)🚶 Crowds: Very High (especially July-August)🎭 Key Events:
- Dragon Boat Festival (June) – Watch traditional boat races on Suzhou Creek.
- Shanghai Book Fair (August) – A huge literary event for book lovers.

### 🍁 Fall (September – November) – Best for Festivals & Mild Weather
✅ Why Visit? Crisp air, golden leaves, and fewer tourists make this a fantastic time to visit. Sightseeing is easy, and it’s less crowded than spring.
🌡️ Temperature: 55-80°F (13-27°C)🚶 Crowds: Moderate (busiest during Golden Week)🎭 Key Events:
- Mid-Autumn Festival (September-October) – Time for mooncakes and lantern displays.
- Golden Week (Oct 1-7) – A massive national holiday; expect extreme crowds at attractions.
- Shanghai Jazz Festival (October) – A must for music lovers.
🛑 Avoid: October 1-7 (Golden Week) – Domestic tourism skyrockets, making flights, hotels, and attractions insanely packed.
### ❄️ Winter (December – February) – Cold & Least Crowded
✅ Why Visit? If you want cheaper hotels, empty tourist sites, and cozy winter food, this is your season. Expect cold but rare snowfall.
🌡️ Temperature: 35-50°F (2-10°C)🚶 Crowds: Lowest of the year (except during Chinese New Year)🎭 Key Events:
- Christmas & New Year’s Eve Celebrations – Shanghai’s expat bars & malls go all out.
- Chinese New Year (late Jan/early Feb) – Huge fireworks, temple fairs, and lion dances.
💡 Tip: Try hotpot restaurants (Haidilao or Little Sheep) to warm up and experience local culture.
## Shanghai Travel Pass & Budgeting Tips 💳
Shanghai is one of the most affordable major cities in the world for public transportation, but costs can vary depending on your travel style. Here’s a detailed breakdown of expenses and money-saving hacks to help you budget smartly while exploring the city.
## 💰 Daily Budget Estimates for Travelers
Travel StyleBudget ($/day)What You GetBackpacker$30-$50Hostels, local street food, metro, free attractions.Mid-Range$60-$120Boutique hotels, restaurants, metro/taxis, paid attractions.Luxury$200+5-star hotels, fine dining, private drivers, premium experiences.
## 🚇 Shanghai Public Transport Card (Jiaotong Card) – The Best Way to Get Around
💳 Where to Buy It?
- Metro stations, convenience stores (FamilyMart, Lawson), and Pudong Airport.
- Deposit: ¥20 ($3 USD), refundable when returning the card.
- Top-Up Amount: Minimum ¥10 (~$1.40), but load at least ¥50 ($7 USD) for a few days.
💡 Pro Tip: The Jiaotong Card saves you from fumbling with cash and offers small fare discounts on multiple rides.
## 💵 Cost of Transportation in Shanghai
🚇 Shanghai Metro (Best for tourists)
- Fare Range: ¥3-6 ($0.50-$1 USD) per ride
- Hours: 5:30 AM – 11:30 PM
- Best Lines for Tourists:
Line 2 (Connects Pudong Airport to downtown)
Line 10 (French Concession, Yu Garden, Xintiandi)
Line 11 (Disneyland)
🚖 Taxis & Didi (China’s Uber)
- Starting Fare: ¥14 ($2 USD) for first 3 km
- Per KM Rate: ¥2.5 ($0.35 USD) after 3 km
- Night Surcharge (11 PM-5 AM): 30% extra
- Didi App: Similar to Uber, but cheaper than taxis. Download Didi (滴滴出行) and use WeChat Pay or Alipay for payment.
🚌 Buses
- Fare: ¥2 ($0.30 USD) per ride
- Slower than metro, but useful for scenic routes (e.g., sightseeing along the Bund).
⛴️ Huangpu River Ferry (Cheapest Way to See the Skyline)
- Fare: ¥2-5 ($0.30-$0.70 USD)
- Route: Crosses the Huangpu River, great for budget travelers who want Bund views for cheap.
## 🍜 Budgeting for Food in Shanghai
🔥 Must-Try Cheap Eats:
- Jia Jia Tang Bao (佳家汤包) – Legendary soup dumplings, ¥20 ($3 USD).
- Yang’s Fried Dumplings (小杨生煎) – Crispy-bottomed dumplings, ¥10-15 ($2 USD).
- Shengjian Bao (生煎包) – Fried pork buns, ¥8-12 ($1.50 USD).

## 💳 Money-Saving Tips for Shanghai
✅ Get a Jiaotong Card – Saves time & offers small fare discounts.✅ Use Metro Over Taxis – Taxis get stuck in traffic, metro is faster & cheaper.✅ Eat at Local Spots – Avoid expensive tourist traps near Nanjing Road.✅ Avoid Peak Season Prices – Hotel & flight prices skyrocket during Golden Week & Chinese New Year.✅ Use WeChat Pay or Alipay – Cash isn’t used much in Shanghai; digital payments are king.

### Shanghai on a Budget? Here’s Your $50/Day Plan:
- 🛌 Stay in a clean hostel (~$15).
- 🍜 Eat dumplings & street food (~$10).
- 🚇 Get a Jiaotong Card & use metro (~$3).
- 🎟️ Pick one main attraction per day (~$10).
- Enjoy free activities (walking the Bund, French Concession, temples).
## 1. The Bund
The Bund is one of the most popular attractions in Shanghai.
## 2. Yu Garden
Just south of the Bund lies a magnificent display of classical Chinese architecture—the Yu Garden. The Yu Garden is a collection of ponds, rockeries, and shops in a Chinese-style bazaar. This garden dates back to the 1500s, during the golden years of the Ming Dynasty. I also bought my favorite souvenir, an engraved pair of chopsticks, at the bazaar.
Yu Garden
## 3. Tianzifang and Xintiandi
Located in the French Concession of Shanghai, Tianzifang and Xintiandi are trendy neighborhoods with boutique shops, bars, and restaurants. Tianzifang is known for its bustling narrow streets and Shanghai Shikumen buildings.
Xintiandi, another pedestrian-friendly zone, is a more modern, but equally lively, neighborhood in the heart of Shanghai. Together, both Tianzifang and Xintiandi reflect the city’s French influence.
Tianzifang is one of the top attractions in Shanghai.
## 4. Shanghai Museum
The Shanghai Museum is China’s premier museum of classical Chinese art. This free museum in the People’s Square offers a glimpse of China’s ancient civilization and rich culture. With over 120,000 historical artifacts—including ancient sculptures, paintings, and bronzeware—the Shanghai Museum is a must-visit in Shanghai!
Shanghai Museum, People’s Square
## 5. Oriental Pearl Tower
The Oriental Pearl Radio & Television Tower is the most iconic structure of Shanghai’s skyline. Standing 1,535 feet (468 meters) tall, this tower serves as a broadcasting center, observation deck, and hotel. If you wish to visit the Oriental Pearl Tower observation decks, I strongly recommend booking online in advance.
Oriental Pearl Tower
## 6. Jing’an Temple
The Jing’an Temple is a Buddhist temple complex built nearly 800 years ago. Inside, you will find traditional Chinese structures, white jaded halls, and monks that bring the temple to life. It also has the largest sitting jade Buddha statue in China (fun fact).
Surrounded by luxury shopping malls and skyscrapers, this historic temple stands as a sharp contrast to the modern and bustling city.
Jing’an Temple provides a stark contrast from the ultra-modern buildings surrounding it.
## 7. Nanjing Road
Nanjing Road is the main pedestrian street in Shanghai and one of the busiest shopping streets in the world. Spanning 3 miles (5 kilometers) between the Jing’an District and the Bund, Nanjing Road contains hundreds of high-end shops, hotels, and restaurants. This street is also home to several historic shops tracing back to the Qing Dynasty— including clock, medicine, and jewelry boutiques.
Words of advice: this street can be extremely packed, especially during holidays and weekends. If you wish to avoid the crowds, I recommend visiting during lunchtime (noon to 1pm).
Rain or shine, Nanjing Road is a bustling commercial center.
## Shanghai is truly a state-of-the-art city
Contrary to Western perceptions from decades past, China is not merely a nation of remote villages traversed by three-wheeled carts. Shanghai is a modern, innovative, and bustling city.
READ: 33 Things to Do Before a Flight!
Nanjing Road comes to life at night.
## China travel tips and advice
- Choosing a Tour Operator: China is not particularly a backpacking or do-it-yourself type of destination. As such, I recommend booking your trip through a tour company or travel agency that specializes in China. Remote Lands is a top provider of luxury travel in Asia, and curates excellent itineraries for travelers seeking to experience China’s culture and charm.
- Processing Your Visa in Advance: Be sure to refer to the Chinese Embassy and consulate websites for visa information and requirements. I recommend utilizing a visa processing service in order to ensure reliable and timely processing. In order to obtain a 10-year visa, I went through Orient Destinations, an efficient and trustworthy agency that is a registered visa agent by the New York Chinese Consulate.
- Planning Your Itinerary: For first time visitors to China, most travel experts will recommend that you visit Shanghai, Beijing, and Xi’an. Each of these destinations contain established tourism industries, and are safe and easily accessible.
Yu Garden is one of the top attractions in the heart of Shanghai.
## Day Trips from Shanghai
Shanghai is an incredible city, but if you have extra time, taking a day trip adds a whole new dimension to your experience. Within 1-2 hours, you can explore ancient water towns, scenic lakes, historic temples, and cultural hubs—all offering a refreshing contrast to Shanghai’s modern skyline.
Here are the best day trips from Shanghai, how to get there, and what to do when you arrive.
### 1. Zhujiajiao Water Town – The “Venice of Shanghai” 🏯
🚆 Travel Time: ~1 hour🚄 How to Get There: Metro Line 17 → Zhujiajiao Station, then a short walk.
Zhujiajiao is one of the best-preserved water towns in China, with 400-year-old stone bridges, canals, and traditional houses. If you want a scenic escape from Shanghai’s skyscrapers, this is the spot.
### 🌟 Top Things to Do in Zhujiajiao:
✅ Take a Wooden Boat Ride – Drift along ancient canals for ¥100 (~$14 USD per boat, fits 6 people).✅ Walk Across Fangsheng Bridge – The largest stone bridge in Zhujiajiao with panoramic canal views.✅ Try Local Street Food – Freshwater crab, Zongzi (sticky rice dumplings), and smoked fish.✅ Explore Kezhi Garden – A beautiful private garden & pavilion from the Qing Dynasty.✅ Shop on North Street – A bustling old street with tea houses, trinkets, and hand-painted fans.
💡 Pro Tip: Visit early morning (before 10 AM) or late afternoon to avoid crowds.
### 2. Hangzhou – West Lake & Tea Plantations 🌿
🚆 Travel Time: ~1 hour by bullet train🚄 How to Get There: Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station → Hangzhou East Railway Station
Hangzhou is famous for West Lake (a UNESCO site), lush tea plantations, and ancient temples. It’s one of China’s most scenic cities, perfect for nature lovers.
### 🌟 Top Things to Do in Hangzhou:
✅ Explore West Lake 🚣 – Walk, rent a bike, or take a boat ride across the lake for unreal sunset views.✅ Visit the Longjing (Dragon Well) Tea Plantations 🍵 – Tour tea fields & sip fresh Longjing tea in the hills.✅ See Leifeng Pagoda 🏯 – Climb for breathtaking views of West Lake & Hangzhou skyline.✅ Check Out Lingyin Temple – One of China’s most important Buddhist temples, with intricate rock carvings.✅ Eat “Beggar’s Chicken” 🍗 – A famous Hangzhou dish where a whole chicken is wrapped in lotus leaves and baked in clay.
💡 Pro Tip: If you only have a half-day, stick to West Lake & the tea plantations.
### 3. Suzhou – The City of Classical Gardens & Silk 🎋
🚆 Travel Time: ~30 minutes by bullet train🚄 How to Get There: Shanghai Railway Station → Suzhou Railway Station
Suzhou is famous for its classical Chinese gardens, ancient canals, and silk production. It’s often called the “Venice of the East” and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
### 🌟 Top Things to Do in Suzhou:
✅ Stroll Through the Humble Administrator’s Garden – The largest classical garden in Suzhou.✅ Visit Tiger Hill Pagoda – A leaning pagoda over 1,000 years old (Suzhou’s version of the Leaning Tower of Pisa).✅ Take a Boat Ride on the Grand Canal – Cruise through ancient waterways lined with traditional houses.✅ Explore Shantang Street – A historic street with silk shops, lantern-lit teahouses, and canal views.✅ Learn About Silk at Suzhou Silk Museum – Discover China’s silk-making history & buy authentic silk scarves.
💡 Pro Tip: Rent a bike to explore Suzhou’s gardens & canals at your own pace.
### 4. Nanjing – History, Temples & Sun Yat-Sen Mausoleum 🏯
🚆 Travel Time: ~1.5 hours by bullet train🚄 How to Get There: Shanghai Railway Station → Nanjing South Railway Station
Nanjing is China’s former capital with deep historical significance, including ancient temples, museums, and the stunning Purple Mountain area.
### 🌟 Top Things to Do in Nanjing:
✅ Visit the Sun Yat-Sen Mausoleum – A huge memorial complex dedicated to China’s founding father.✅ Explore the Nanjing Massacre Memorial – A powerful WWII history museum (a must for history buffs).✅ Climb the Ming City Wall – Walk along the best-preserved Ming Dynasty wall in China.✅ Visit the Confucius Temple (Fuzimiao) – A beautiful temple with scenic river views & street food.✅ Hike Purple Mountain – A nature escape with temples, pagodas, and forested trails.
💡 Pro Tip: Spend a night in Nanjing if you want to hike Purple Mountain & see more sights.
🚆 Travel Time: ~1.5 hours by bullet train + short taxi ride🚄 How to Get There: Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station → Tongxiang Railway Station → Taxi to Wuzhen
Wuzhen is one of China’s most picturesque water towns, with cobblestone streets, arched bridges, and lantern-lit canals. It has a slower, more peaceful vibe than Zhujiajiao.
### 🌟 Top Things to Do in Wuzhen:
✅ Wander the East & West Scenic Areas – Charming canals, old houses, and photo-perfect bridges.✅ See the Night Lanterns – The entire town glows with lanterns at night—super romantic!✅ Visit the Hundred-Bed Museum – Showcases elaborate ancient Chinese beds & furniture.✅ Check Out the Footbinding Culture Museum – Learn about China’s controversial past tradition.✅ Eat Wuzhen-Style Braised Pork – A savory local dish, perfect with a bowl of rice.
💡 Pro Tip: Wuzhen is best for an overnight stay because of its magical nighttime atmosphere.
## Learning a Few Key Phrases for Your Trip to Shanghai:
- Nǐ hǎo – Hello
- Xiè xiè – Thank you
- Nǐ huì shuō yīng yǔ ma? – Do you speak English?
- Duō shao qián? – How much is this?
- Tài guile – Too expensive

China is a fascinating country with a rich culture and heritage. With its civilization dating back over 3,500 years, China has the longest continuous history of any country in the world. Be sure to take lots of pictures, and also live in the moment by soaking in the remarkable culture and scenery.

As someone who spends 3 to 6 months a year in the air, I’m pretty much obsessed with aviation. Over the years, I’ve gotten lost in Doha’s art-filled concourses, sprinted across DFW’s sky train system, and watched the sun rise through the massive glass walls of Istanbul Airport. So when I set out to rank the 13 largest airports in the world by physical size in 2025, I went deep into the data.
## The World’s 13 Largest Airports by Size (At a Glance)
Here’s a quick snapshot of the world’s largest airports. While this gives you the big picture, stick around because there are some crucial details and caveats you won’t want to miss.
